name: Pārsa
caption: Pārsa · the spring audience, c. 470 BC
era: The Persian empire of Xerxes · c. 470 BC

spring.note: rare, memorable showers build over the mountain in the afternoon

summer.note: dust breezes after dry days; the court is away

winter.note: snow on the ridge, few travellers

look.light: crisp mountain air, cool shadows; stone turns honey at dawn and rose at dusk

districts.name: The Hall of a Hundred Columns

stages.label: hoisted and set on its dowel
filed in a basket in the fortification
a new robe for the court
set into the gate's glazed panels
a roof beam laid on the capitals

days_shown.label: A spring day: the audience in the morning

figures.note: his parasol-bearer walks with him; enthroned under a canopy in the audience
appears seated at the pavilion; her kind has no walk

xerxes.title: Xšayāršā
xerxes.text: Xerxes finished what his father began here and built the Gate of All Lands. His inscriptions say Auramazdā made him king. On the Apadāna stairs, the peoples of an empire from the Aegean to the Indus bring him gifts; here he receives them enthroned under a canopy among slender columns.
xerxes.epithet: Xerxes, Great King, King of Kings

amestris.title: Amestris
amestris.text: Wife of Xerxes and mother of the next king. Greek historians told dark stories about her; Persian records tell us more about how royal women lived: they owned estates, travelled with their own staff and sealed their own orders. Here she visits the weavers of her household and sits in the garden pavilion.

artaxerxes.title: Artaxšaça
artaxerxes.text: One day he will finish the Hall of a Hundred Columns. Today he is learning to ride and draw a bow on the plain below the terrace. Greek writers said Persian boys were taught three things: to ride, to shoot and to tell the truth. His exact age in 470 is not known.

maus.title: Mauš
maus.text: His name survives on the Treasury tablets of these very years, the receipts of a working empire. Orders reach him to pay craftsmen partly in weighed silver instead of barley; he seals each payment and files the record. The gifts the delegations bring this morning will pass through his doors.

artemisia.title: Artemisia of Caria
artemisia.text: A Carian queen who commanded ships for Xerxes at Salamis, as Herodotus tells. Here we imagine her climbing the stairway with the Carians, who bring a bull, a shield and a spear on the Apadāna reliefs. Whether she was still alive, or still ruling, in 470 is not known.

darius.title: Dārayavauš
darius.text: Darius chose this mountain foot for a new royal city, raised the terrace and began the Apadāna. He reorganised the empire's satrapies, fixed weights and coinage, completed the canal from the Nile to the Red Sea begun by an Egyptian king, and cut his story into the cliff at Bisitun in three languages.

atossa.title: Atossa
atossa.text: Daughter of one king, wife of another, mother of a third. Greek writers made her powerful and proud. Some scholars think the tablets mention her under the Elamite name Udusana; others are less sure. At dusk she is remembered in the courts of the residential wing her son built.

irtashduna.title: Irtašduna
irtashduna.text: The Fortification tablets show this wife of Darius, a daughter of Cyrus, managing estates, workers and stores in her own name and under her own seal. One order from the king sends her two hundred jars of wine, each a marriš of about ten litres, and a hundred sheep.

parnakka.title: Parnakka
parnakka.text: A great Persian noble whose seal, between 506 and 497, moved barley, wine, sheep and travellers across Fārs. The tens of thousands of clay tablets found in the fortification wall are largely the paperwork of his office: the most detailed record of daily life in the empire.

gobryas_aspathines.title: Gaubaruva and Aspačanā
gobryas_aspathines.text: Carved beside Darius's tomb, each labelled by name and office in three languages: Gobryas, the king's spear-bearer, and Aspathines, who holds the king's battle-axe. His title is usually translated bow-bearer, but its meaning is debated. They were the closest companions of the throne.

auramazda.title: Auramazdā
auramazda.text: Every royal inscription begins with him: creator of earth, sky, people and happiness. The tablets also show offerings to other gods, Iranian and Elamite. The winged figure in a disc above the reliefs may be him, or the king's fortune; scholars still debate it. Known in Iran today as the Faravahar, it is a cherished symbol.
auramazda.epithet: The great god of the inscriptions

tishtrya.title: Tištrya
tishtrya.text: In the Avesta, the star Sirius takes the shape of a white horse with golden ears, fights the drought demon on the shore of the cosmic sea and wins rain for the lands. The hymn was written down many centuries later. Watch the ridge when spring clouds gather.

yima.title: Yima
yima.text: The Avesta's Yima ruled when there was neither heat nor cold, sickness nor death. Medieval Persians, seeing these ruins, believed only he could have built them, and called them the Throne of Jamshid. The storyteller tells old Iranian tales; whether they were told this way in 470 is not known.
yima.epithet: King of the golden age (a tale)

erexsa.title: Ərəxša
erexsa.text: One line of the Avesta remembers him as the swiftest archer of the Aryans, his arrow flying like the rain star. The story of the arrow that set a frontier was told by much later writers. At dusk an arrow's streak crosses the sky over the archery ground.

thraetaona.title: Θraētaona
thraetaona.text: In the Avesta, Θraētaona defeats Aži Dahāka, the three-headed dragon. Much later Ferdowsi retold the tale with new characters; the old hymn is short and fierce, and was itself written down long after Pārsa. Children at the stairway plaza ask for it again and again.

saena.title: Saēna
saena.text: The Avesta names the saēna bird. Later Persian books made it the Simurgh, wise and healing, nesting in the tree of all seeds. The hymns that name it were written down much later. At dawn, sometimes, a great shadow crosses the mountain behind the terrace.

mithradata.title: Miθradāta
mithradata.text: Miθradāta writes in two worlds: Aramaic in ink on soft leather, and checks the Elamite scribes pressing wedges into clay. Every jar of wine, every sack of barley and every traveller's meal on the royal road ends up on one of his tablets, sealed and filed.

rtakama.title: Ṛtakāmā
rtakama.text: Ṛtakāmā leads forty weavers. The tablets show women like her drawing the highest rations in their group, and mothers receiving extra grain after a birth. Her workshop's patterned cloth will become robes for the court and gifts for honoured guests.

hermon.title: Hermon
hermon.text: Hermon came from Ionia to cut stone for the king; at Susa, Darius's building charter names Ionians and Lydians as the stonecutters. He reads a block by the sound it makes under his hammer. Today he shapes a column drum for the new hall, paid partly in barley and partly in weighed silver.

bel_iddin.title: Bēl-iddin
bel_iddin.text: Bēl-iddin's family has made bricks for generations, in Babylon and now in Pārsa; at Susa, Darius's charter says Babylonians made the baked bricks. Mudbricks dry in the sun for walls; the best are fired and glazed in blue and yellow. He stamps each mould with a careful thumb.

pediese.title: Pediese
pediese.text: Pediese beats gold into leaf thin enough to float, for door fittings and the edges of painted reliefs; at Susa, Darius's charter names Medes and Egyptians as goldsmiths. He also makes armlets with griffin heads like the ones the Lydians bring as gifts.

manes.title: Manes
manes.text: Manes fits cedar beams that travelled from Lebanon, across rivers and over mountains, to rest on the bull capitals; at Susa, Darius's charter names Sardians and Egyptians as woodworkers. Up on the scaffold the whole plain lies below him, green with young barley.

farnadata.title: Farnadāta
farnadata.text: Farnadāta checks every traveller's sealed travel document, the halmi of the tablets, then hands out flour, beer and fodder by the day. Express riders change horses here without stopping to talk. His scribes log every ration, so we know what a journey cost.

irdumartiya.title: Irdumartiya
irdumartiya.text: Irdumartiya, the Elamite rendering of the Persian name Ṛtavardiya, grows barley along the canal. A share of every harvest goes to the royal stores, and from there back out as rations for the workers on the terrace. When the water is his turn, he opens the channel at dawn.

dadush.title: Daduš and Udusana
dadush.text: Daduš and his sister count the delegations climbing the stairs: today the Lydians brought a chariot and the Elamites a lioness with two cubs. They are not allowed on the terrace. They watch from the plaza anyway, and stay for the storyteller at dusk.

apadana.title: Apadāna
apadana.text: Darius began it and Xerxes finished it: a hall of 36 columns, 19.5 m tall, with porticoes of twelve on three sides. In the hall and the north portico the capitals carry paired bulls on tall volutes; in the west portico, which you see, bulls sit straight on the fluted shaft, and lions in the east. The north stair's central panel shows the king enthroned.

great_stair.title: The great stairway
great_stair.text: Each side climbs 63 shallow steps to a landing and 48 more to the top: 111 steps of 10 cm, 38 cm deep and 6.70 m wide, easy enough to climb in a long robe or leading a horse. Delegations come up here behind their ushers on audience mornings.

apadana_stair_n.title: The north stair of the Apadāna
apadana_stair_n.text: Its reliefs climb in three registers: guards, staff-bearers and nobles on one wing, the gift-bearing peoples on the other, lions attacking bulls in the corners. In 470 its central panel shows the king enthroned, the crown prince behind him; later it was replaced by guards under a winged disc.

apadana_stair_e.title: The east stair of the Apadāna
apadana_stair_e.text: Twenty-three delegations climb its reliefs in three registers, each led by the hand by a Persian or Median usher, each with its gifts: a lioness and cubs, a chariot, gold dust, a dromedary. Their names and order are partly guessed; the cards say probably where scholars disagree.

tacara_stair_s.title: The Tačara's south stair
tacara_stair_s.text: The stair to Darius's palace is carved with guards and gift-bearers in procession and an inscription naming the builder. The decorated west stair is later: in 470 that side is plain.

hadish_stair_w.title: The Hadiš stair
hadish_stair_w.text: Its reliefs show servants carrying food up to the king: lambs, wineskins, covered dishes. At dusk, real servants climb it with the king's dinner.

tripylon_stair.title: The Tripylon stair
tripylon_stair.text: Persian and Median nobles climb its reliefs side by side, holding flowers, turning to talk, a hand on a friend's shoulder: the most human scene on the terrace.

gate_all_lands.title: Duvarθi visadahyu
gate_all_lands.text: Xerxes's own name for it: the gate of all lands. Four columns over 16.5 m tall carry kneeling bulls; plain bulls stride out of the west door, and human-headed winged bulls, an old Mesopotamian guardian, crown the east. Every visitor to the terrace passes through.

tacara.title: Tačara
tacara.text: Darius's own word for his building, in the inscription on its walls: "I built this tačara". A small palace of polished dark stone with twelve columns, its portico and relief stair facing south. Door reliefs show the king walking under a parasol.

hadish.title: Hadiš
hadish.text: Xerxes's palace on the highest platform: 36 columns and a portico of twelve. Its stair reliefs show servants carrying food, wineskins and young goats up to the king's table, as the servants here still do at dusk.

tripylon.title: Tripylon
tripylon.text: A small hall with three doors linking the palaces and the audience halls. On its stair, Persian and Median nobles climb holding flowers, chatting, a hand on a friend's shoulder. It may not yet be finished in 470; Shahbazi gives it to Xerxes and Artaxerxes I.

hall_100.title: Hall of a Hundred Columns
hall_100.text: Begun by Xerxes and finished by his son, a grid of ten by ten columns nearly 14 m tall. Today some stand finished, others rise drum by drum under timber cranes. The portico's capitals are human-headed bulls, and two colossal bulls are still being roughed out at its door.

treasury.title: The Treasury
treasury.text: Low mudbrick halls with wooden columns plastered and painted in patterns. Gifts, silver and tribute were weighed and stored here; its tablets of 492-458 record wages paid partly in silver. Later the audience relief from the Apadāna stair was moved here, where archaeologists found it.

harem.title: The residential wing
harem.text: Rows of apartments around courts, with small columned halls and stone door frames showing the king. The name harem is modern; who lived here, royal women, officials or stores, is debated.
harem.epithet: Called the harem by its excavators

garrison.title: Garrison quarters
garrison.text: Rooms for the royal guard, an armoury and a courtyard for drill behind the terrace. The Greeks called the king's guard the Immortals; their Persian name is unknown. Spearmen march out from here at every change of the watch.

south_stores.title: Southern storerooms
south_stores.text: Long rooms for jars of wine, oil and grain, sealed and recorded like everything else in Pārsa. The court fed thousands: a Greek list of the king's dinner counts sheep, geese and sacks of flour by the hundred.

cistern.title: The cistern
cistern.text: A basin cut into the mountain feeds channels that run under the terrace. Drains in the stone carried rain off the platform; after a spring shower they spout into the plain.

quarry.title: The quarry
quarry.text: Grey limestone is cut from the mountain behind the terrace: a line marked, a slot cut, wedges driven, a block levered free. Wedge holes and half-cut blocks are still there today. Follow a block from here to the new hall.

paradise_gate.title: The glazed gate
paradise_gate.text: A gate faced with glazed bricks, bulls and dragons in yellow and white on blue, like Babylon's Ishtar Gate. The real one stood 3.5 km to the west, built under Cyrus or Cambyses; the game sets it in the garden wall.

pavilion.title: The garden pavilion
pavilion.text: An open columned pavilion where the garden's stone channels cross. Carpets inside, cypress rows on every side, almond and pomegranate in flower. At night musicians play here.

road_station.title: Royal-road station
road_station.text: A walled yard with stables, a storeroom and a room for the official. Travellers show a sealed document and receive the day's flour, beer and fodder; riders find fresh horses waiting.

naqsh_cliff.title: Naqsh-e Rostam
naqsh_cliff.text: Darius's tomb is a cross cut into the cliff: a palace front with four columns, and above it the king before a fire altar, standing on a throne carried by thirty figures of his peoples. Inscriptions in three languages tell what kind of king he wished to be.
naqsh_cliff.epithet: Tomb of Darius (the name is medieval)

kaba.title: The square tower
kaba.text: A tall square stone tower with blind windows and a single high door, facing Darius's tomb. Its date and purpose are debated: a tomb, a fire house, a store for royal records? No one knows.

terrace.title: The terrace
terrace.text: A platform of fitted grey limestone against the mountain, raised by Darius and about twelve metres high on its long west face, topped by stepped merlons. Everything on it was painted: red floors, patterned robes on the reliefs, gold on the crowns.

fort_wall.title: The fortification
fort_wall.text: Mudbrick walls with square towers climb the slope behind the terrace. Inside them excavators found the Fortification tablets: tens of thousands of receipts for rations, travel and work from the years 509 to 493.

new_year.title: A New Year at Pārsa?
new_year.text: The Persian year began with the month Ādukanaiša, near the spring equinox. Many scholars, among them the Iranian historian Shapur Shahbazi, think this terrace was built for the New Year, the festival later called Nowruz; others answer that no ancient text says so and that the reliefs show an ideal, timeless empire. The name Nowruz first appears centuries later, in Middle Persian. Whether today's Nowruz, loved by many millions, reaches back to these stairs, no one can yet prove.

susa_charter.title: An empire of many peoples
susa_charter.text: Darius's building inscription at Susa names who made his palace there: stonecutters from Ionia and Sardis, goldsmiths from Media and Egypt, Babylonians for the baked bricks, cedar from Lebanon carried by Carians and Ionians. Pārsa was built the same way, by workers of many lands, some of whom had come far from home not by choice.

archives.title: The paperwork of an empire
archives.text: Tens of thousands of clay tablets, most in Elamite, some in Aramaic, recorded every ration, journey and payment in Fārs. Each was sealed, dried in the sun and filed in baskets. Together they are the most detailed record of daily life in the ancient Near East.

royal_road.title: The royal road
royal_road.text: Stations at fixed stages from Sardis to Susa, with rations for anyone carrying a sealed document and fresh horses for the king's riders. Herodotus, a Greek outsider, wrote admiringly that nothing mortal travels faster than these messengers, passing the message from rider to rider.

paradise.title: Paradise
paradise.text: The Elamite tablets call such estates partetaš; the Old Persian word is reconstructed as paridaida. The Greeks borrowed it as paradeisos, and English made it paradise: a walled garden of channels, orchards and shade, its water opened turn by turn at dawn.

guardians.title: Borrowed guardians
guardians.text: Human-headed winged bulls came from Assyria, the cavetto cornices over the doors from Egypt, the stone-cutting skills from Ionia and Lydia. The Persian kings took the art of every people they ruled and made it their own, a new style meant to show an empire at peace.

religion.title: Fire and the gods
religion.text: Fire altars stand before the king on the reliefs, and magi tend them at dawn. Herodotus wrote that Persians used no altars and no fire in sacrifice, a Greek outsider's claim the reliefs contradict. Kings honoured many gods, yet Xerxes's own inscription boasts of destroying a sanctuary of false gods: tolerance had limits.

standards.title: Weights and canals
standards.text: Ten shekels made a karša of about 83 grams, and silver was weighed, not counted; Darius's gold darics were rare in Fārs. His inscriptions by the Red Sea boast of a canal from the Nile, begun by an Egyptian king, that carried ships to Persia.

takht_e_jamshid.title: Takht-e Jamshid
takht_e_jamshid.text: Medieval Persians, finding the ruins, named them for the legendary king Jamshid, the Yima of the Avesta. The name is about 1,500 years later than the moment shown here; the city's own name was Pārsa, like the land and its people.

qanat.title: Water under the plain
qanat.text: A line of shaft mounds marks a tunnel leading groundwater to the fields. Such qanats were known in the empire, one dated in Achaemenid Egypt, but none at Pārsa is dated to 470: the game shows one as a reasonable guess.

rations.title: Rations and wages
rations.text: Workers drew monthly rations of barley, with wine, beer or sheep for higher grades; by now part was paid in weighed silver. The tablets show mothers given extra grain after a birth, twice as much for a boy, and women overseers drawing the highest rations.

law.title: The king's law
law.text: Darius's inscriptions speak of his dāta, his law, and of rewarding the loyal and punishing the liar. Greek writers mention royal judges. In a portico a dispute is heard: two workmen and an official in Median dress, talking it through until they agree.

kurtash.title: The kurtaš
kurtash.text: The tablets call the workers kurtaš: men, women and children of many origins, with families, names and regular rations. Some were hired, some deported, some attached to estates; their status varied and is debated. The game shows them as they were in the tablets: working people. They built Pārsa.

courtier.title: Persian noble
courtier.text: In a long pleated robe and a fluted cap, he attends the audience and walks the terrace with a friend, as the nobles do on the Tripylon stair.

usher.title: Usher
usher.text: In Median dress, staff in hand, the usher leads each delegation by the hand up to the king and presents it.

spearman.title: Spearman of the guard
spearman.text: Robed, with a tall spear whose butt is a silver pomegranate and a bow on his back. Greeks called the king's guard the Immortals.

mede_guard.title: Guard in Median dress
mede_guard.text: Tunic, trousers and a bow case on the hip; at night he walks the wall with a torch.

magus.title: Magus
magus.text: The tablets call them makuš. Hood drawn over the mouth, a bundle of twigs in hand, he feeds the fire at dawn and dusk.

servant.title: Servant of the court
servant.text: Carries water to the kitchens by day and dishes up the Hadiš stair at dusk, as on its reliefs.

household_woman.title: Woman of a royal household
household_woman.text: The tablets show royal women with households of their own: weavers, cooks and stewards who come and go between the courts.

musician.title: Court musician
musician.text: An angular harp, pipes or a frame drum; Greek writers say many women sang and played at the Persian court.

quarryman.title: Quarryman
quarryman.text: Marks a line, cuts a slot, drives the wedges and levers a block free of the mountain.

mason.title: Mason
mason.text: Squares and dresses each drum in the yard, then sees it slung, hoisted and set on its dowel.

carpenter.title: Carpenter
carpenter.text: Saws and fits cedar beams for the roof of the new hall, high on the scaffold.

sculptor.title: Relief sculptor
sculptor.text: Sketches in red, roughs out, models and smooths: a procession of figures in calm profile.

scribe.title: Scribe
scribe.text: Presses wedges into damp clay, rolls a seal across it and leaves it in the sun to dry.

porter.title: Porter
porter.text: Carries sacks from the threshing floors and the stores to the granary yard.

weaver.title: Weaver
weaver.text: Works an upright loom in a workshop of women; her cloth becomes robes for the court.

brickmaker.title: Brickmaker
brickmaker.text: Mixes clay with straw and water, fills a wooden mould and lays the bricks in rows to dry.

wall_decorator.title: Wall decorator
wall_decorator.text: At Susa, Darius's charter says Medes and Egyptians decorated the walls. Here they set glazed bricks into the gate's bulls and dragons.

goldsmith.title: Goldsmith
goldsmith.text: Melts, hammers, punches and polishes gold for door fittings, armlets and vessels.

dyer.title: Dyer
dyer.text: Soaks wool in vats of madder, woad and weld by the canal, then rinses and hangs it.

grinder.title: Grinder
grinder.text: Grinds barley on a saddle quern, sifts it and bags the flour for the ovens.

baker.title: Baker
baker.text: Slaps rounds of dough on the inside wall of a tanūr oven and peels them off, crisp.

child.title: Child
child.text: The tablets list rations for boys and girls. They run by the canal, play knucklebones and watch the delegations.

elamite_priest.title: Elamite priest
elamite_priest.text: Pours offerings for Humban and other Elamite gods, whom the tablets show the state supplied.

gardener.title: Gardener of the paradise
gardener.text: Opens the channels at dawn, waters, plants and prunes the royal orchards.

farmer.title: Farmer
farmer.text: Hoes young barley along the canals; a share of his harvest goes to the royal stores.

groom.title: Groom
groom.text: Waters, brushes and exercises the horses, which draw rations of their own in the tablets.

nisaean_horse.title: Nisaean horse
nisaean_horse.text: The famous horses of Media, tails tied, forelocks bunched in a topknot.

archer.title: Archer
archer.text: Strings his bow, draws, looses and walks to the butts to collect his arrows.

shepherd.title: Shepherd
shepherd.text: Leads the flock out at dawn with a dog and brings it home to the fold at dusk.

hoopoe.title: Hoopoe
hoopoe.text: A crested, barred bird probing the garden beds for grubs, calling hoo-poo-poo.

station.title: Station scribe
station.text: Reads each traveller's sealed document and logs the flour, beer and fodder issued.

delegation_medes.title: Medes
delegation_medes.text: Neighbours and partners of the Persians. They bring a pitcher, bowls, a short sword, rings and a riding costume of coat and trousers, the dress half the court itself wears.

delegation_elamites.title: Elamites
delegation_elamites.text: From the old kingdom of Susa and Anšan. Wreathed, without hats, they bring two bows, two daggers and a lioness with her two cubs.

delegation_armenians.title: Armenians
delegation_armenians.text: From the high valleys of the north. Hooded riders, they lead a bridled stallion and carry a vessel with griffin-headed handles.

delegation_parthians.title: Parthians
delegation_parthians.text: From the steppe edge east of the Caspian. In face-protecting hoods they bring two bowls and a two-humped camel.

delegation_babylonians.title: Babylonians
delegation_babylonians.text: From the great city on the Euphrates. In tasselled caps they bring shallow bowls, a fringed garment and a humped bull.

delegation_lydians.title: Lydians
delegation_lydians.text: From Sardis, where the Royal Road begins. In tall conical hats they bring metal phials, griffin-headed armlets and a small two-horse chariot.

delegation_arians.title: Arians
delegation_arians.text: Probably from Haraiva, around Herat. Dust-hooded, in short cloaks and trousers, they bring bowls and a camel.

delegation_syrians.title: Syrians
delegation_syrians.text: Livius calls them Syrians; other works say Assyrians. They bring bowls, a copper ingot shaped like an ox hide, a tasselled garment and two rams.

delegation_cappadocians.title: Cappadocians
delegation_cappadocians.text: From the Anatolian uplands. Their cloaks are pinned at the shoulder; they lead a stallion and bring a coat and trousers.

delegation_saka.title: Saka
delegation_saka.text: Riders of the northern steppes in tall pointed hoods. They lead a horse with a bell and bring rings, a coat and trousers; their leader wears sword and bow.

delegation_egyptians.title: Egyptians
delegation_egyptians.text: From the Nile. Their panel on the stair is damaged; traces of a hippopotamus remain. The game shows them in white linen.

delegation_ionians.title: Yaunā
delegation_ionians.text: Ionian Greeks, dressed like the Lydians but bareheaded. They bring ribbed cups, shallow bowls, folded cloth and round bundles, perhaps balls of thread.

delegation_bactrians.title: Bactrians
delegation_bactrians.text: From beyond the Hindu Kush, wreathed and earringed. They bring bowls and a two-humped camel.

delegation_gandharans.title: Gandharans
delegation_gandharans.text: From the Kabul and Indus valleys. They bring lances, a shield and a water buffalo.

delegation_arachosians.title: Arachosians
delegation_arachosians.text: Probably from around Kandahar. With tasselled wreaths and earrings they bring bowls and a camel.

delegation_sagartians.title: Sagartians
delegation_sagartians.text: Probably horse-breeding nomads of the Iranian plateau. Hooded riders, they lead a stallion and bring garments.

delegation_sogdians.title: Sogdians
delegation_sogdians.text: Probably from around Samarkand; the panel is damaged. In tight caps they bring a sword, rings, battle-axes and a stallion.

delegation_indians.title: Indians
delegation_indians.text: From Hinduš on the Indus. Bare-chested, they carry baskets of gold dust on a shoulder pole and lead a mule.

delegation_thracians.title: Thracians
delegation_thracians.text: Skudra, from across the Hellespont, in felt caps. They bring spears, round shields and a stallion.

delegation_arabs.title: Arabs
delegation_arabs.text: From the desert's edge, in long tasselled robes. They lead a dromedary, the one-humped camel of Arabia.

delegation_carians.title: Carians
delegation_carians.text: From the Aegean coast of Anatolia, wreathed like Lydians. They bring a round shield, a spear and a bull.

delegation_libyans.title: Libyans
delegation_libyans.text: Probably from Cyrene's hinterland; the panel is damaged. They bring an oryx and a chariot.

delegation_kushites.title: Kushites
delegation_kushites.text: From Kush up the Nile. They bring an elephant tusk, a small lidded bowl and an animal often read as an okapi, though the identification is debated.

strings.first_visit: Pārsa, around the spring equinox of 470 BC. The barley is green, snow lies on the mountain, and the first delegation is forming up at the foot of the stair.
strings.audience: The spring audience begins: three delegations climb the great stair.
strings.guard_change: A horn: the guard changes at the stairway and the Gate.
strings.ration_day: Ration day: barley and bread are handed out at the granary yard.
strings.storyteller: At the stairway plaza an old storyteller begins a tale.
strings.tishtrya: Spring rain. On the ridge, for a moment, a white horse.
strings.caravan: A caravan comes down the Royal Road at dusk.
strings.harvest: The harvest offering at the threshing floor.
strings.fire_evening: The fire evening: people gather at the altars on the terrace.
strings.decorate_zone: A walled plot in the paradise, with channels to lay and trees to plant.
